entries.466e51039fe8dbe3ceb413f312c41e12be721be4: <div sID="gen10551" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Ps.13" sID="Ps.13"/> <div eID="gen10551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10552" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10553" type="x-p"/> This psalm is the deserted soul's case and cure. Whether it was penned upon any particular occasion does not appear, but in general, I. David sadly complains that God had long withdrawn from him and delayed to relieve him, <reference osisRef="Ps.13.1-Ps.13.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. He earnestly prays to God to consider his case and comfort him, <reference osisRef="Ps.13.3-Ps.13.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. He assures himself of an answer of peace, and therefore concludes the psalm with joy and triumph, because he concludes his deliverance to be as good as wrought, <reference osisRef="Ps.13.5-Ps.13.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>.
entries.4ff20b85ec1226f0d2a386cc86617cd347d44030: <div eID="gen10553" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10552" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Complaints and Prayers Turned into Praises.</title> <div sID="gen10554" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> How long wilt thou forget me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me? <hi type="super">2</hi> How long shall I take counsel in my soul, <hi type="italic">having</hi> sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me? <hi type="super">3</hi> Consider <hi type="italic">and</hi> hear me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> my God: lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the <hi type="italic">sleep of</hi> death; <hi type="super">4</hi> Lest mine enemy say, I have prevailed against him; <hi type="italic">and</hi> those that trouble me rejoice when I am moved. <hi type="super">5</hi> But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation. <hi type="super">6</hi> I will sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because he hath dealt bountifully with me. <div eID="gen10554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10555" type="x-p"/> David, in affliction, is here pouring out his soul before God; his address is short, but the method is very observable, and of use for direction and encouragement. <div eID="gen10555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10556" type="x-p"/> I. His troubles extort complaints (<reference osisRef="Ps.13.1-Ps.13.2">v. 1, 2</reference>); and the afflicted have liberty to <hi type="italic">pour out their complaint before the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1">Ps. cii.</reference> <hi type="italic">title.</hi> It is some ease to a troubled spirit to give vent to its griefs, especially to give vent to them at the throne of grace, where we are sure to find one who is afflicted in the afflictions of his people and is troubled with the feeling of their infirmities; thither we have boldness of access by faith, and there we have <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">parresia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">freedom of speech.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen10556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10557" type="x-p"/> 1. What David complains of. (1.) God's unkindness; so he construed it, and it was his infirmity. He thought God had forgotten him, had forgotten his promises to him, his covenant with him, his former lovingkindness which he had shown him and which he took to be an earnest of further mercy, had forgotten that there was such a man in the world, who needed and expected relief and succour from him. Thus Zion said, <hi type="italic">My God has forgotten me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.14">Isa. xlix. 14</reference>), Israel said, <hi type="italic">My way is hidden from the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.27">Isa. xl. 27</reference>. Not that any good man can doubt the omniscience, goodness, and faithfulness of God; but it is a peevish expression of prevailing fear, which yet, when it arises from a high esteem and earnest desire of God's favour, though it be indecent and culpable, shall be passed by and pardoned, for the second thought will retract it and repent of it. God hid his face from him, so that he wanted that inward comfort in God which he used to have, and herein was a type of Christ upon the cross, crying out, <hi type="italic">My God, why hast thou forsaken me?</hi> God sometimes hides his face from his own children, and leaves them in the dark concerning their interest in him; and this they lay to heart more than any outward trouble whatsoever. (2.) His own uneasiness. [1.] He was racked with care, which filled his head: <hi type="italic">I take counsel in my soul;</hi> "I am at a loss, and am <hi type="italic">inops consilii—without a friend to advise with</hi> that I can put any confidence in, and therefore am myself continually projecting what to do to help myself; but none of my projects are likely to take effect, so that I am at my wits' end, and in a continual agitation." Anxious cares are heavy burdens with which good people often load themselves more than they need. [2.] He was overwhelmed with sorrow, which filled his heart: <hi type="italic">I have sorrow in my heart daily.</hi> He had a constant disposition to sorrow and it preyed upon his spirits, not only in the night, when he was silent and solitary, but by day too, when lighter griefs are diverted and dissipated by conversation and business; nay, every day brought with it fresh occasions of grief; <hi type="italic">the clouds returned after the rain.</hi> The bread of sorrow is sometimes the saint's daily bread. Our Master himself was a man of sorrows. (3.) His enemies' insolence, which added to his grief. Saul his great enemy, and others under him, were exalted over him, triumphed in his distress, pleased themselves with his grief, and promised themselves a complete victory over him. This he complained of as reflecting dishonour upon God, and his power and promise. <div eID="gen10557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10558" type="x-p"/> 2. How he expostulates with God hereupon: "<hi type="italic">How long</hi> shall it be thus?" And, "Shall it be thus <hi type="italic">for ever?</hi>" Long afflictions try our patience and often tire it. It is a common temptation, when trouble lasts long, to think it will last always; despondency then turns into despair, and those that have long been without joy begin, at last, to be without hope. "Lord, tell me how long thou wilt hide thy face, and assure me that it shall not be for ever, but that thou wilt return at length in mercy to me, and then I shall the more easily bear my present troubles." <div eID="gen10558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10559" type="x-p"/> II. His complaints stir up his prayers, <reference osisRef="Ps.13.3-Ps.13.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. We should never allow ourselves to make any complaints but what are fit to be offered up to God and what drive us to our knees. Observe here, <div eID="gen10559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10560" type="x-p"/> 1. What his petitions are: <hi type="italic">Consider</hi> my case, <hi type="italic">hear</hi> my complaints, and <hi type="italic">enlighten my eyes,</hi> that is, (1.) "Strengthen my faith;" for faith is the eye of the soul, with which it sees above, and sees through, the things of sense. "Lord, enable me to look beyond my present troubles and to foresee a happy issue of them." (2.) "Guide my way; enable me to look about me, that I may avoid the snares which are laid for me." (3.) "Refresh my soul with the joy of thy salvation." That which revives the drooping spirits is said to <hi type="italic">enlighten the eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.27">1 Sam. xiv. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.8">Ezra ix. 8</reference>. "Lord, scatter the cloud of melancholy which darkens my eyes, and let my countenance be made pleasant." <div eID="gen10560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10561" type="x-p"/> 2. What his pleas are. He mentions his relation to God and interest in him (<hi type="italic">O Lord my God!</hi>) and insists upon the greatness of the peril, which called for speedy relief and succour. If his eyes were not enlightened quickly, (1.) He concludes that he must perish: "I shall <hi type="italic">sleep the sleep of death;</hi> I cannot live under the weight of all this care and grief." Nothing is more killing to a soul then the want of God's favour, nothing more reviving than the return of it. (2.) That then his enemies would triumph: "<hi type="italic">Lest my enemy say,</hi> So would I have it; lest Saul, lest Satan, be gratified in my fall." It would gratify the pride of his enemy: He will say, "<hi type="italic">I have prevailed,</hi> I have gotten the day, and been too hard for him and his God." It would gratify the malice of his enemies: They will <hi type="italic">rejoice when I am moved.</hi> And will it be for God's honour to suffer them thus to trample upon all that is sacred both in heaven and earth? <div eID="gen10561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10562" type="x-p"/> III. His prayers are soon turned into praises (<reference osisRef="Ps.13.5-Ps.13.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): But <hi type="italic">my heart shall rejoice and I will sing to the Lord.</hi> What a surprising change is here in a few lines! In the beginning of the psalm we have him drooping, trembling, and ready to sink into melancholy and despair; but, in the close of it, rejoicing in God, and elevated and enlarged in his praises. See the power of faith, the power of prayer, and how good it is to draw near to God. If we bring our cares and griefs to the throne of grace, and leave them there, we may go away like Hannah, and our <hi type="italic">countenance will be no more sad,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.18">1 Sam. i. 18</reference>. And here observe the method of his comfort. 1. God's mercy is the support of his faith. "My case is bad enough, and I am ready to think it deplorable, till I consider the infinite goodness of God; but, finding I have that to trust to, I am comforted, though I have no merit of my own. In former distresses <hi type="italic">I have trusted in the mercy of God,</hi> and I never found that it failed me; his mercy has in due time relieved me and my confidence in it has in the mean time supported me. Even in the depth of this distress, when God hid his face from me, when without were fightings and within were fears, yet <hi type="italic">I trusted in the mercy of God</hi> and that was as an anchor in a storm, by the help of which, though I was tossed, I was not overset." And still <hi type="italic">I do trust in thy mercy;</hi> so some read it. "I refer myself to that, with an assurance that it will do well for me at last." This he pleads with God, knowing what pleasure he takes <hi type="italic">in those that hope in his mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.147.11">Ps. cxlvii. 11</reference>. 2. His faith in God's mercy filled his heart with <hi type="italic">joy in his salvation;</hi> for joy and peace come <hi type="italic">by believing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.15.13">Rom. xv. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Believing, you rejoice,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.8">1 Pet. i. 8</reference>. Having put his trust in the mercy of God, he is fully assured of salvation, and that his heart, which was now daily grieving, should <hi type="italic">rejoice in that salvation.</hi> Though weeping endure long, joy will return. 3. His joy in God's salvation would fill his mouth with songs of praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.13.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will sing unto the Lord,</hi> sing in remembrance of what he has done formerly; though I should never recover the peace I have had, I will die blessing God that ever I had it. He has dealt bountifully with me formerly, and he shall have the glory of that, however he is pleased to deal with me now. I will sing in hope of what he will do for me at last, being confident that all will end well, will end everlastingly well." But he speaks of it as a thing past <hi type="italic">(He has dealt bountifully with me</hi>), because by faith he had received the earnest of the salvation and he was as confident of it as if it had been done already. <div eID="gen10562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10563" type="x-p"/> In singing this psalm and praying it over, if we have not the same complaints to make that David had, we must thank God that we have not, dread and deprecate his withdrawings, sympathize with those that are troubled in mind, and encourage ourselves in our most holy faith and joy.  <chapter eID="Ps.13"/> <div eID="gen10563" type="x-p"/>

entries.4b5a7a5a186c1a195623ae51bcf24c3af0f2830d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5573"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.13.1-Ps.13.6">Psa 13:1-6</reference>. On title, see Introduction. The Psalmist, mourning God's absence and the triumph of his enemies, prays for relief before he is totally destroyed, and is encouraged to hope his trust will not be in vain.</title> <div sID="gen8459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5573"/>1. The forms of expression and figure here used are frequent (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.12">Psa 9:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">10:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen8459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">How long ... for ever--</hi>Shall it be for ever? <div eID="gen8460" type="x-p"/>
entries.2811347be5e20090e9b9d2da0790a58abb53ceb4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5574"/><div sID="gen8461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5574"/>2. The counsels or devices of his heart afford no relief. <div eID="gen8461" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffa73d596aef66000dc928f036586abb295eec3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5575"/><div sID="gen8462" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5575"/><hi type="bold">3. lighten mine eyes--</hi>dim with weakness, denoting approaching death (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.27-1Sam.14.29">1Sa 14:27-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.7">Psa 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.10">38:10</reference>). <div eID="gen8462" type="x-p"/>
entries.302321b9dae040d51ebc56eb2b68067fdcac6cf6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5576"/><div sID="gen8463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5576"/><hi type="bold">4. rejoice--</hi>literally, "shout as in triumph."<div eID="gen8463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am moved--</hi>cast down from a firm position (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.6">Psa 10:6</reference>). <div eID="gen8464" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9dfa5ea37ef294f865a353a8e5b336d996d55a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5577"/><div sID="gen8465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5577"/>5-6. Trust is followed by rejoicing in the deliverance which God effects, and, instead of his enemy, he can lift the song of triumph. <chapter eID="Ps.13"/>

entries.10d859172da7404429a817fbb35c3c074e7839c3: <div eID="gen18695" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18696" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18697" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18697" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18696" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18698" type="x-p"/> This Psalm contains the sentiments of an afflicted soul that earnestly desires succor from the Lord. The psalmist complains of delay, <reference osisRef="Psa.13.1-Psa.13.3">Psa 13:1-3</reference>; prays for light and comfort, because he finds himself on the brink of death, <reference osisRef="Psa.13.3">Psa 13:3</reference>; dreads the revilings of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.13.4">Psa 13:4</reference>; anticipates a favorable answer, and promises thanksgiving, <reference osisRef="Psa.13.5">Psa 13:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.13.6">Psa 13:6</reference>. <div eID="gen18698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18699" type="x-p"/> There is nothing particular in the inscription. The Psalm is supposed to have been written during the captivity, and to contain the prayers and supplications of the distressed Israelites, worn out with their long and oppressive bondage. <div eID="gen18699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18700" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18701" type="x-p"/> How long wilt thou forget me - The words עד אנה ad anah, to what length, to what time, translated here how long? are four times repeated in the two first verses, and point out at once great dejection and extreme earnestness of soul. <div eID="gen18701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18702" type="x-p"/> Hide thy face from me? - How long shall I be destitute of a clear sense of thy approbation?
entries.52296ee4a9aafd102c7437d0d2363c10caad5763: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18703" type="x-p"/> Take counsel in my soul - I am continually framing ways and means of deliverance; but they all come to naught, because thou comest not to my deliverance. When a soul feels the burden and guilt of sin, it tries innumerable schemes of self-recovery; but they are all useless. None but God can speak peace to a guilty conscience. <div eID="gen18703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18704" type="x-p"/> Mine enemy be exalted - Satan appears to triumph while the soul lies under the curse of a broken law.
entries.b6966013ac37ea155d857c956b5e119ec9384186: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18705" type="x-p"/> Consider and hear me - Rather, answer me. I have prayed; I am seeking thy face I am lost without thee; I am in darkness; my life draws nigh to destruction; if I die unforgiven, I die eternally. O Lord my God, consider this; hear and answer, for thy name's sake.
entries.bfae36b91828ccebd12481863281e6eb7e87c2a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18706" type="x-p"/> Let mine enemy say - Satan's ordinary method in temptation is to excite strongly to sin, to blind the understanding and inflame the passions; and when he succeeds, he triumphs by insults and reproaches. None so ready then to tell the poor soul how deeply, disgracefully, and ungratefully it has sinned! Reader, take heed. <div eID="gen18706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18707" type="x-p"/> When I am moved - When moved from my steadfastness and overcome by sin. O what desolation is made by the fall of a righteous soul! Itself covered with darkness and desolation, infidels filled with scoffing, the Church clad in mourning, the Spirit of God grieved, and Jesus crucified afresh, and put to an open shame! O God, save the pious reader from such wreck and ruin!
entries.da240f20ea4f431617f1a5c42b85653c09ff73ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18708" type="x-p"/> But I have trusted in thy mercy - Thou wilt not suffer me to fall; or if I have fallen, wilt thou not, for his sake who died for sinners, once more lift up the light of thy countenance upon me? Wilt thou not cover my sin? <div eID="gen18708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18709" type="x-p"/> My heart shall rejoice in thy salvation - There is no true joy but of the heart; and the heart cannot rejoice till all guilt is taken away from the conscience.
entries.05daf792e309d79b1c372b106b5e12e8f7d28d47: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen18709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18710" type="x-p"/> I will sing unto the Lord - That heart is turned to God's praise which has a clear sense of God's favor. <div eID="gen18710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18711" type="x-p"/> Because he hath dealt bountifully with me - כי גמל עלי ki gamel alai, because he hath recompensed me. My sorrows were deep, long continued, and oppressive, but in thy favor is life. A moment of this spiritual joy is worth a year of sorrow! O, to what blessedness has this godly sorrow led! He has given me the oil of joy for the spirit of heaviness, and the garments of praise for mourning. <div eID="gen18711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18712" type="x-p"/> The old MS. Psalter, which I have so frequen,tly mentioned and quoted, was written at least four hundred years ago, and written probably in Scotland, as it is in the Scottish dialect. That the writer was not merely a commentator, but a truly religious man, who was well acquainted with the travail of the soul, and that faith in the Lord Jesus Christ which brings peace to the troubled heart, is manifested from various portions of his comment. To prove this I shall, I think I may say, favor the reader with another extract from this Psalm on the words, "How long wilt thou forget me," etc., <reference osisRef="Psa.13.1">Psa 13:1</reference>. I have only to observe that with this commentator a true penitent, one who is deeply in earnest for his salvation, is called a "perfyte man"; i.e., one wholly given up to God. <div eID="gen18712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18713" type="x-p"/> How lang lord for getes thu me in the endyng? How lang o way turnes thou thi face fro me? The voice of haly men that covaytes and yernes the comyng of Iehu Crist, that thai might lyf with hym in ioy; and pleynaund tham of delaying. And sais, Lord how lang for getes the me in the endyng? That I covayte to haf and hald. That es how lang delayes thu me fra the syght of Iehu Crist, that es ryght endyng of myn entent. And how lang turnes thu thi face fra me? that es, qwen wil thu gif me perfyte Knawing of the? This wordes may nane say sothly, bot a perfyte man or woman, that has gedyrd to gydir al the desyres of thair Saule, and with the nayle of luf fested tham in Iehu Crist. Sa tham thynk one hour of the day war our lang to dwel fra hym; for tham langes ay til hym; bot tha that lufs noght so, has no langyng that he come: for thair conscience sais thaim, that thai haf noght lufed hym als that suld have done." <div eID="gen18713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18714" type="x-p"/> The language of true Christian experience has been the same in all times and nations. "But he that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love;" and to such this is strange language.  <chapter eID="Ps.13"/> <div eID="gen18714" type="x-p"/>

entries.ad4ae1e0f1112dceae82d31283bb3cd3f7d07c49: <reference osisRef="Ps.13.1-Ps.13.2">Psa 13:1-2</reference> (Heb.: 13:2-3) The complicated question: till when, how long...for ever (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.10">Psa 74:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.79.5">Psa 79:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.47">Psa 89:47</reference>), is the expression of a complicated condition of soul, in which, as Luther briefly and forcibly describes it, amidst the feeling of anguish under divine wrath “hope itself despairs and despair nevertheless begins to hope.” The self-contradiction of the question is to be explained by the conflict which is going on within between the flesh and the spirit. The dejected heart thinks: God has forgotten me for ever. But the spirit, which thrusts away this thought, changes it into a question which sets upon it the mark of a mere appearance not a reality: how long shall it seem as though Thou forgettest me for ever? It is in the nature of the divine wrath, that the feeling of it is always accompanied by an impression that it will last for ever; and consequently it becomes a foretaste of hell itself. But faith holds fast the love that is behind the wrath; it sees in the display of anger only a self-masking of the loving countenance of the God of love, and longs for the time when this loving countenance shall be again unveiled to it. Thrice does David send forth this cry of faith out of the inmost depths of his spirit. To place or set up contrivances, plans, or proposals in his soul, viz., as to the means by which he may be able to escape from this painful condition, is equivalent to, to make the soul the place of such thoughts, or the place where such thoughts are fabricated (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.26.24">Pro 26:24</reference>). One such עצה chases the other in his soul, because he recognises the vanity of one after another as soon as they spring up. With respect to the יומם which follows, we must think of these cares as taking possession of his soul in the night time; for the night leaves a man alone with his affliction and makes it doubly felt by him. It cannot be proved from <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.16">Eze 30:16</reference> (cf. Zep 2:4 בּצּהרים), that יומם like יום (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.25">Jer 7:25</reference>, short for יום יום) may mean “daily” (Ew. §313, <hi type="italic">a</hi>). יומם does not mean this here, but is the antithesis to לילה which is to be supplied in thought in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.13.3">Psa 13:3</reference></hi>. By night he proposes plan after plan, each one as worthless as the other; and by day, or all the day through, when he sees his distress with open eyes, sorrow (יגון) is in his heart, as it were, as the feeling the night leaves behind it and as the direct reflex of his helpless and hopeless condition. He is persecuted, and his foe is in the ascendant. רוּם is both to be exalted and to rise, raise one’s self, i.e., to rise to position and arrogantly to assume dignity to one’s self (<hi type="italic">sich brüsten</hi>). The strophe closes with <hi type="italic">‛ad - āna</hi> which is used for the fourth time.
entries.90212ce62a674de56cd37be00250cc7b26ce05bf: <reference osisRef="Ps.13.3-Ps.13.4">Psa 13:3-4</reference> (Heb.: 13:4-5) In contrast to God’s seeming to have forgotten him and to wish neither to see nor know anything of his need, he prays: הבּיטה (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Isa 63:15</reference>). In contrast to his being in perplexity what course to take and unable to help himself, he prays: ענני, answer me, who cry for help, viz., by the fulfilment of my prayer as a real, actual answer. In contrast to the triumphing of his foe: האירה עיני, in order that the triumph of his enemy may not be made complete by his dying. To lighten the eyes that are dimmed with sorrow and ready to break, is equivalent to, to impart new life (Ezr 9:8), which is reflected in the fresh clear brightness of the eye (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.27">1Sa 14:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.29">1Sa 14:29</reference>). The lightening light, to which האיר points, is the light of love beaming from the divine countenance, Psa 31:17. Light, love, and life are closely allied notions in the Scriptures. He, upon whom God looks down in love, continues in life, new powers of life are imparted to him, it is not his lot to sleep the death, i.e., the sleep of death, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">Jer 51:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.57">Jer 51:57</reference>, cf. Psa 76:6. המּות is the accusative of effect or sequence: to sleep so that the sleep becomes death (lxx εἰς θάνατον), Ew. §281, <hi type="italic">e.</hi> Such is the light of life for which he prays, in order that his foe may not be able at last to say יכלתּיו (with accusative object, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.38.5">Jer 38:5</reference>) = יכלתּי לו, <reference osisRef="Ps.129.2">Psa 129:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.32.26">Gen 32:26</reference>, I am able for him, a match for him, I am superior to him, have gained the mastery over him. כּי, on account of the future which follows, had better be taken as temporal (<hi type="italic">quum</hi>) than as expressing the reason (<hi type="italic">quod</hi>), cf. בּמוט רגלי, Psa 38:17.
entries.c5e3e09b4263809a46f8a9bfdf4c2e6075a6abfb: <reference osisRef="Ps.13.5-Ps.13.6">Psa 13:5-6</reference> (Heb.: 13:6) Three lines of joyous anticipation now follow the five of lament and four of prayer. By יאני he sets himself in opposition to his foes. The latter desire his death, but he trusts in the mercy of God, who will turn and terminate his affliction. בּטח בּ denotes faith as clinging fast to God, just as חסה בּ denotes it as confidence which hides itself in Him. The voluntative יגל pre-supposes the sure realisation of the hope. The perfect in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.13.6">Psa 13:6</reference></hi> is to be properly understood thus: the celebration follows the fact that inspires him to song. גּמל על to do good to any one, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.7">Psa 116:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.17">Psa 119:17</reference>, cf. the radically cognate (על) גּמר Psa 57:3. With the two iambics <hi type="italic">gamal‛alaj</hi>the song sinks to rest. In the storm-tossed soul of the suppliant all has now become calm. Though it rage without as much now as ever - peace reigns in the depth of his heart. Prayer for Protection against Wicked, Crafty Men <div eID="gen9147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9148" type="x-p"/> The close of the preceding Psalm is the key to David’s position and mood in the presence of his enemies which find expression in this Psalm. He complains here of serpent-like, crafty, slanderous adversaries, who are preparing themselves for war against him, and with whom he will at length have to fight in open battle. The Psalm, in its form more bold than beautiful, justifies its לדוד in so far as it is Davidic in thoughts and figures, and may be explained from the circumstances of the rebellion of Absalom, to which as an outbreak of Ephraimitish jealousy the rebellion of Sheba ben Bichri the Benjamite attached itself. <reference osisRef="Ps.58.1-Ps.58.11">Psa 58:1-11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.64.1-Ps.64.10">Psa 64:1-10</reference> are very similar. The close of all three Psalms sounds much alike, they agree in the use of rare forms of expression, and their language becomes fearfully obscure in style and sound where they are directed against the enemies.  <chapter eID="Ps.13"/> <div eID="gen9148" type="x-p"/>

entries.00d82b17600a147044f84229fe9985923db1e392:
PSALM 13.
The subject of this psalm is almost the same as that of the preceding. David, being afflicted, not only with the deepest distress, but also feeling himself, as it were, overwhelmed by a long succession of calamities and multiplied afflictions, implores the aid and succor of God, the only remedy which remained for him; and, in the close, taking courage, he entertains the assured hope of life from the promise of God, even amidst the terrors of death.
To the chief musician. A song of David.
Psalm 13:1-2
1. How long, O Jehovah, wilt thou forget me, for ever? How long wilt thou hide thy face from me? 2. How long shall I take counsel in my soul? and have sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?
 
1. How long, O Jehovah. It is very true that David was so greatly hated by the generality of people, on account of the calumnies and false reports which had been circulated against him, that almost all men judged that God was not less hostile to him than Saul
It was the opinion of Theodoret that this psalm was composed by David, not during his persecution by Saul, but when Absalom conspired against him; and the reason which he assigns for this opinion is, “that the trouble which Saul gave him was before his great sin, and so he was full of confidence; but that of Absalom was after it, which made him cry out in this doleful manner.” — Bishop Patrick’s Paraphrase on the Book of Psalms.
and his other enemies were. But here he speaks not so much according to the opinion of others, as according to the feeling of his own mind, when he complains of being neglected by God. Not that the persuasion of the truth of God’s promises was extinguished in his heart, or that he did not repose himself on his grace; but when we are for a long time weighed down by calamities, and when we do not perceive any sign of divine aid, this thought unavoidably forces itself upon us, that God has forgotten us. To acknowledge in the midst of our afflictions that God has really a care about us, is not the usual way with men, or what the feelings of nature would prompt; but by faith we apprehend his invisible providence. Thus, it seemed to David, so far as could be judged from beholding the actual state of his affairs, that he was forsaken of God. At the same time, however, the eyes of his mind, guided by the light of faith, penetrated even to the grace of God, although it was hidden in darkness. When he saw not a single ray of good hope to whatever quarter he turned, so far as human reason could judge, constrained by grief, he cries out that God did not regard him; and yet by this very complaint he gives evidence that faith enabled him to rise higher, and to conclude, contrary to the judgment of the flesh, that his welfare was secure in the hand of God. Had it been otherwise, how could he direct his groanings and prayers to him? Following this example, we must so wrestle against temptations as to be assured by faith, even in the very midst of the conflict, that the calamities which urge us to despair must be overcome; just as we see that the infirmity of the flesh could not hinder David from seeking God, and having recourse to him: and thus he has united in his exercise, very beautifully, affections which are apparently contrary to each other. The words, How long, for ever? are a defective form of expression; but they are much more emphatic than if he had put the question according to the usual mode of speaking, Why for so long a time? By speaking thus, he gives us to understand, that for the purpose of cherishing his hope, and encouraging himself in the exercise of patience, he extended his view to a distance, and that, therefore, he does not complain of a calamity of a few days’ duration, as the effeminate and the cowardly are accustomed to do, who see only what is before their feet, and immediately succumb at the first assault. He teaches us, therefore, by his example, to stretch our view as far as possible into the future, that our present grief may not entirely deprive us of hope.
